newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Privatisation law to clear Kuwait parliament - MP.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation law to clear Kuwait parliament - MP.

text.p: A draft law sanctioning the privatisation of Kuwait's public utilities could pass parliament before the end of June, a leading MP said on Wednesday.
"It might be achieved," head of parliament's finance committee Nasser al-Sanea told Reuters. "The bill could pass parliament before the end of the current session (June)."

Parliament, which has voiced repeated concern over the future of Kuwaiti employees, is studying a 45-section draft law to privatise a variety of basic services including water and electricty with telephones on the top of the list.

Sanea, addressing a seminar on Wednesday on the privatisation of telephones, said parliament "will never pass a law which could harm Kuwaiti workers and does not include very clear guarantees for the future of Kuwaiti employees."

Parliament earlier this month "found it appropriate" to reject a previous separate bill to privatise telephones for lack of such guarantees and measures to ensure competition in the self-regulated state monopoly.
Also "the state's assets were undervalued...The rejection was a must," Sanea told the seminar which was organised by the Ministry of Communications.

Officials later told Reuters that the state considered the value of the assets as a secret but said the rejected bill had called for the formation of a 150 million dinar ($493 million) telephones company as a first step towards the privatisation of the heavily-subsidised sector.

"Local calls are being subsidised by international calls," Mahdy al-Jazzaf, an adviser to parliament on the privatisation of telephones, said. "There are about 400,000 telephone lines in Kuwait with each line earning about $700 but costing $550."

Officials at the seminar told Reuters that the Communications Ministry, including transport and post, rougly earned between 70-80 million dinars a year while expenditure was between 60-70 million. "The margin is very small," one said.
Jazzaf, a techno-economics researcher, also said that the ministry had a surplus of workers, employing 5,800 people while only 3,000 were needed to do the job, according to 1995 figures.
Talk of possible layoffs once the telephones sector is privatised angered the head of the ministry's workers' union.
"Privatisation is unemployment. It leads to poverty which in turn leads to higher crime rates and even poses a threat to the system of rule," Badr al-Najd said in an emotional response.
He accused the ministry's top officials of mismanagement.

Ministers often say that efforts to balance the budget and reform the economy clash with the high expenditure on salaries of government employees, almost half of the state's annual budget of some $14 billion.

Currently the subsidised public services are used as employment centres for Kuwaitis. The state employs some 92 percent of Kuwaitis in the work force and provides them with high salaries and generous benefits compared to foreigners of the same grade working in Kuwait.
The latest privatisation draft law contains several detailed proposals to compensate Kuwaitis in case of a rise in the cost of services and layoffs, officials and MP say.
